description: I'm Dan Lee-Odinson, a Space Studies undergraduate and technical program manager, developing AI-assisted aerospace software and research projects. I'm building an accessible lunar-mission planning browser using AI-driven development, scientific computing, and data visualization. My focus is rigorous systems engineering, reproducible results, and making lunar exploration accessible to everyone. The moon belongs to us all.
summary:
Common Horizon: A Sunrise on Humanity's Next Frontier

Common Horizon is a web app that helps a mission planner choose where and when to land on the Moon. Pick a landing site, a launch date and the hardware to deliver, and it shows where the Sun and the Earth sit against that site's real horizon through the stay: how long the site is lit, how long it can talk to Earth, and whether the power system makes it through the dark. Slip the launch by days and the ranking of seventeen sites reorders.

The horizon decides the answer. At the Shackleton Connecting Ridge, a smooth-Moon calculation puts the Sun in view for 57 percent of 2027. With the ridge's real terrain from NASA's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter, the same point has the Sun in view for about 83 percent of the year, and its longest dark period falls from 140 days to about a week.

Every site is drawn on real ground from NASA LOLA and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter data, and a mission assistant answers questions using only the engine's results. Sun and Earth positions come from NASA ephemeris data and agree with NASA's JPL Horizons System to within 0.006 degrees.
details:
Live site: https://commonhorizon.study
Code: https://github.com/dan-lee-odinson/common-horizon (public, Apache-2.0)

What it does

The challenge asks for an intuitive way to compare landing sites and dates by where the Sun and the Earth are relative to the horizon, because those two angles set a mission's power and its direct link to Earth. Common Horizon answers in three stages inside one continuous 3D view.

  1. Orbit. The Moon, with its surface from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, the direction of the Sun and the Earth at its true size in the sky, with clocks in UTC and in lunar time.
  2. Mission select. Seventeen preset sites, from the Apollo landings to this decade's commercial deliveries and the south polar ridges, or any latitude and longitude. The planner picks hardware, a launch date and a stay length, and the sites are ranked on sunlight, Earth contact, landing slope and power. Each requirement reads pass, fail or not known. A launch-delay control shows how a slip of days reorders the ranking.
  3. Site. Down on the surface, the mission's hardware stands at true scale on the real ground. The ground's shape comes from NASA LOLA heights through NASA Moon Trek at all seventeen presets, and its surface from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter's wide-angle camera mosaic. A chart draws the Sun's path against the skyline, a bar across the stay shows each lit and dark period, and a Site map panel opens the same place in Moon Trek and in LROC QuickMap.

A mission assistant sits beside all three stages. It answers plain-language questions about the mission on screen ("the launch slipped 14 days, which site ranks first now?") from the engine's results for that mission. It never changes the planner, and it says so when the results do not cover a question.

How it works

  • Positions. A physics engine in Python reads four NASA NAIF SPICE kernels and gives the Sun's and the Earth's position in the Moon's body-fixed frame for any time, then turns each into azimuth and elevation at the site.
  • The horizon. For each site, the skyline is computed from NASA LOLA elevation models: every half degree of azimuth, with the Moon's curvature included, on the 40-meter polar model near the site and the 240-meter model beyond it. Skylines are stored for six sites so far: Shackleton Connecting Ridge, the Nobile region, IM-1, IM-2, the Draper SERIES-2 site and Chandrayaan-3.
  • Visibility. The Sun's and the Earth's discs are compared with the skyline hour by hour, for an observer 2 meters above the ground. A body counts as visible when any part of its disc clears the terrain.
  • The planner. A hardware catalog holds each figure with its source and a status label (NASA figure, company figure or our estimate). It checks whether a payload fits a lander, and whether the power sources and storage carry the loads through day and night.
  • Landing slope. For each preset, the slope of the best-fit plane to LOLA heights within 500 meters of the site, from NASA Moon Trek, is compared with the lander's published limit where one exists. Where a lander has no published limit, the app says "not known" and gives no pass or fail.
  • The ground you see. For every preset the Site view loads two height grids from Moon Trek's LOLA layers: 10-meter spacing across 1.28 km and 250-meter spacing across 64 km with the Moon's curvature included, drawn at true scale. Over them lies a surface picture: the LRO wide-angle camera mosaic at fifteen sites, and at the ridge and Nobile, where that mosaic is mostly permanent shadow, a relief picture worked out from LOLA heights.
  • The mission assistant. One route on the service runs the same evaluation the page shows and passes its results to OpenAI's open-weight gpt-oss-120b model on Amazon Bedrock, which words the answer. The model receives no other data and produces no figure of its own.
  • The app. A FastAPI service on AWS Lambda and a React and three.js website on AWS Amplify. The live site runs on the real physics engine: every figure on screen is computed by the service at the moment it is asked.

What the sunlight figures include. At the six sites with stored skylines the sunlight figures use the real terrain. At the other eleven presets they use a smooth horizon, and the app says so on the site's own panel, beside the height the drawn terrain reaches there (as much as 14 degrees at Apollo 17).

Three reference missions

The team's mission planner wrote three reference missions as test cases. Each was run on the live site through its own planner controls.

  • Mission 1, a crewed base stay (Starship HLS, Surface Habitat, a 40 kWe fission unit and one solar array mast) at the Shackleton Connecting Ridge, launched 15 January 2027. Ranked first of seventeen. Sun in view 93.8% of a 30-day stay, 76.1% of 90 days, 68.6% of 180 days and 82.0% of 365 days. The longest dark period grows from 27 hours to 157 hours. Power margin 50% at every stage. Launched 14 days late, the 30-day stay drops to 79.4%, its longest dark period grows to 104 hours, and the ridge falls to fourth.
  • Mission 2, a Griffin cargo delivery with a science rover in the Nobile region, launched 11 August 2027 for a 14-day stay. On time: Sun in view 100%, slope 7.6 degrees against Griffin's 10-degree limit, a pass, ranked first. Launched 14 days late: 26% sunlight, 248 hours of darkness, a fail on night power, ranked last. The ridge takes first place.
  • Mission 3, a cargo stay on solar power and 240 kWh of storage at the Apollo 11 site, launched 7 February 2027 for 30 days. Fails on night power: 353 hours of darkness and a margin of -97%. Adding the 40 kWe fission unit turns the margin to +97%.

Mission 2 is the challenge's question in one picture: the same site and hardware pass or fail on the launch date alone.

How we checked it

  • Against JPL Horizons. For all seventeen preset sites, every hour of 2027, the engine's direction to the Sun differs from Horizons' by at most 0.006 degrees and its direction to the Earth by at most 0.0002 degrees. The Sun's disc is 0.53 degrees wide. The backend can also run the same comparison live, for any place and minute.
  • Against NASA Moon Trek. The engine's Sun directions are also compared with Moon Trek's Sun angle service for the same sites and hours. The largest difference is 0.0066 degrees.
  • The assistant. Seven questions were put to the live assistant and each answer was compared with the engine's results for the same mission. Every figure it gave was the engine's. It declined a question the data does not cover, an instruction to state a false figure, and an off-topic request.
  • Two horizon codes. The team wrote the horizon calculation twice, separately, with different code and different LOLA models. At the Shackleton Connecting Ridge the two skylines differ by a median of 0.01 degrees.
  • Sensitivity. The result moves with the elevation model. At the ridge, the 240-meter model alone gives 89 percent, and counting terrain closer to the observer gives 80 percent. We quote the 40-meter result, about 83 percent and 155 hours, as uncertain by several points either way. Terrain smaller than a pixel, such as boulders, is not modeled.
  • Published work. Gläser et al. (2014) report 92 percent at 2 meters for a location on the same ridge over a 19-year cycle. Their abstract gives no coordinates, so the two points cannot be matched.

Across all of 2027, the Shackleton Connecting Ridge has the Sun in view 83% of the time with terrain against 57% on a smooth Moon, with a longest dark period of 155 hours, the Earth in view 50% of the time and a longest gap in Earth contact of 324 hours. The Nobile region has 49% with terrain against 51% without, a longest dark period of 532 hours, the Earth in view 63% of the time and a longest gap of 246 hours. Terrain also costs sunlight at the two Intuitive Machines sites: 46% against 51% at IM-2 and 39% against 50% at IM-1.

Intended impact

A planner sees in one view what usually takes several tools: the ephemeris, the terrain, the landing slope and the hardware's power budget. The terrain result is the one that changes decisions. Two sites four degrees apart differ by more than two weeks in their longest dark period, and a launch slip can move a short stay out of sunlight. Because every hardware figure carries its source and status, a reader can tell a NASA measurement from a company's claim and from our own estimate. The same view serves an educator or a curious visitor: the Moon, the Sun and the Earth are drawn where they really are, at true size.

What is creative about it

  • One continuous view from orbit to the surface. The visitor never leaves the 3D scene: the Moon in orbit, the ranked sites on its face, then a dive to the ground with the hardware at true scale.
  • The launch slip as a slider. The challenge describes planners re-evaluating when schedules slip. Dragging the delay reorders seventeen sites as you watch, and each row names the requirement that broke.
  • Hardware and power, not only angles. The Sun and Earth angles feed a power budget for real planned hardware, so the answer reads as "this mission survives the night here" or "it does not".
  • Honest labels. Every figure says where it came from, and the app says which sunlight figures include terrain and which do not.
  • An assistant held to the engine. It can explain a result in plain language and cannot invent a number.

What we considered

  • Who uses it. Mission planners who need the figures, and educators and the public who need to see why the south pole is hard.
  • Real terrain against a smooth Moon. Near the pole the Sun stays within a degree or two of the skyline, so a smooth-Moon answer can be wrong by months.
  • Sources and status. No lander in the catalog has flown its mission yet, so each figure is labeled as a NASA figure, a company figure or our estimate.
  • What an AI may and may not do. No figure in the app comes from an AI model, and generated shapes are labeled as illustrations.
  • Scale and honesty in the picture. Hardware, ground, Sun and Earth are drawn at true size, and the app says where a drawing is an illustration.

What we hope to achieve

First, terrain in the sunlight figures at every site. The ground is already drawn at all seventeen presets; the skyline calculation behind the figures covers six. Our first estimate is that terrain costs up to about 5 percent of the sunlight in a lunar day at the most mountainous of the other eleven, the Apollo 17 valley. After that: on-demand skylines for any point, landing hazards at the scale of a lander's footprint, relay satellites for sites that never see the Earth, the mission plan's remaining site criteria such as distance to permanently shadowed ice, and NASA's Coordinated Lunar Time once the standard is set. The repository's README carries the full wishlist. We want a first-pass tool that a student, a mission designer or a curious visitor can open in a browser and trust, because its numbers trace to NASA data.

Tools, languages and software

  • Languages: Python 3.12, TypeScript, JavaScript.
  • Engine and service: SpiceyPy, NumPy, rasterio, FastAPI, Pydantic, Uvicorn, boto3, pytest, Docker.
  • Mission assistant: OpenAI gpt-oss-120b (open weights, Apache 2.0) on Amazon Bedrock.
  • Website: React 19, three.js, React Three Fiber, drei, GSAP, Tailwind CSS, Vite, Vitest, Playwright.
  • 3D models: eleven, all checked with the Khronos glTF Validator. Five are built by our own scripts with three.js from published dimensions, one is a community CAD model, and five are shapes generated by TRELLIS.2 (Microsoft) from pictures and scaled to a published height or, where none is published, to our labeled estimate.
  • Terrain and surface files: Python with NumPy, rasterio and Pillow, from NASA Moon Trek.
  • Demo video: Playwright, FFmpeg and Remotion, recording the live site by script.
  • Hosting: AWS Lambda (a container image in Amazon ECR), AWS Amplify and Amazon Bedrock, with GitHub Actions running the tests before every deployment.
  • Fonts: Oxanium, Geist and Geist Mono (SIL Open Font License).

Use of SI/AI

The team chose the challenge, the idea and the scope. SI/AI tools helped write and review software and text, generated five 3D shapes and parts of the demo video, and word the mission assistant’s answers. They also laid out options for design decisions, and the team chose among them.

Who used what

  • Dan (website, planner, hardware models, terrain and surface files, stored skylines): Claude and Claude Code (Anthropic), models Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2. They wrote code and tests under his direction, reviewed pull requests, prepared the Moon, terrain and surface files from NASA data, ran the JPL Horizons check and drafted this text for his edit.
  • Isabella (physics engine): ChatGPT (OpenAI), model GPT-6, assisting with engine code.
  • Alexandru (backend service): Claude Code (Anthropic), model Claude Opus 5.5, drafting backend code, tests and documents, with OpenAI Codex as an independent reviewer.
  • Cam (mission planning): Muse (Meta), model Muse Spark 1.3, to cross-check the sources and figures in his research, for translation between English and French and reading support, and to review each revision of the mission plan. The mission ideas and decisions are his and the team's.

Inside the app

  • The mission assistant is the one place a language model runs in the app: OpenAI's gpt-oss-120b on Amazon Bedrock. It words its answers from the engine's results for the mission on screen and produces no figure of its own. Its panel says it answers in text only and never changes the planner.
  • Five of the eleven 3D hardware models are shapes generated by TRELLIS.2 (Microsoft), run on fal.ai, from pictures: three NASA illustrations and renderings (the VIPER rover, a habitation module and a fission power unit) and two of a team member's own photographs of display models (the crew rover and the pressurized rover). The finished shapes carry no logos, lettering or insignia. Each is labeled "illustrative shape, SI/AI-generated from a photo; not the manufacturer's data" in its file and on the models page, with the picture's credit and the request id.
  • No figure in the app comes from an AI model. Positions, skylines, slopes, sunlight and power results are computed by our code from NASA data, and the checks above compare them with JPL Horizons, with Moon Trek and with each other. The app contains no AI-generated images, video or audio.

In the demo video

  • The six-second title sequence was generated with Gen-4.5 (Runway) and upscaled with FLUX Video Upscale (Black Forest Labs). It carries a visible "SI/AI-generated" mark.
  • The music is "Cosmic Swells", an instrumental track generated with Suno (model v6) from a text description written by the team. That is stated in the video's description and in the video file's tags.
  • Everything else in the video is a recording of the running site, captured by a script, and a closing team card made by hand by a team member.

Where it is acknowledged: commit messages carry an "SI/AI" line naming the tool and model, and the repository holds two AI-use logs (docs/AI_USE_LOG.md and backend/docs/AI_USE_LOG.md) and a sources file for each part of the project.

How the NASA data is used

  • JPL Horizons System. The independent check of our engine: apparent azimuth and elevation of the Sun and the Earth for observers at all seventeen preset sites, every hour of 2027, retrieved through the Horizons API on 15 November 2026. The backend also asks Horizons live and returns its answer beside the engine's for any place and minute.
  • NASA NAIF SPICE kernels: naif0012.tls, de440s.bsp, moon_pa_de440_200625.bpc and moon_de440_250416.tf. Every Sun and Earth position in the engine comes from these.
  • NASA Moon Trek. Four uses: the height grids behind the real ground in the Site view at all seventeen presets; the surface pictures laid over that ground, from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter wide-angle camera mosaics (credit NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University); the LOLA elevation patches behind each preset's landing slope; and Moon Trek's Sun angle service as a second check of the engine's Sun directions. The Site map panel also draws Moon Trek's map tiles.
  • LOLA elevation models from NASA Goddard's Planetary Geodesy Data Archive (LDEM_80S_40MPP_ADJ, LDEM_80S_80MPP_ADJ, LDEM_60S_240MPP_ADJ) and the global 118-meter model from the USGS Astrogeology Science Center. Every terrain skyline comes from these.
  • CGI Moon Kit (NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio): the Moon's surface in the app. Blue Marble Next Generation (credit Reto Stöckli, NASA Earth Observatory): the Earth's surface in the Orbit view.
  • NSSDC and CLPS pages: the Apollo presets and the commercial delivery sites. NASA Technical Reports Server: hardware and power figures, each labeled in the catalog. NASA's "Lunar Site Selection" white paper: the south polar seasons shown in the app.
  • NASA images as the starting pictures for three generated hardware shapes, and NASA's Artemis II photograph art002e021278 on the video's thumbnail.

Partner data and other references

  • ISRO: the Chandrayaan-3 landing site (69.373° S, 32.319° E), a preset site with a stored skyline.
  • JAXA: the SLIM landing site (13.316° S, 25.251° E), a preset site, and the size of JAXA's crewed pressurized rover, which sets the scale of that model.
  • Papers: Barker et al. (2023), Gläser et al. (2014), Mazarico et al. (2011), Ashby and Patla (2024), and Burke, Howard and Kessler (AIAA ASCEND 2022).
  • Company figures for landers and rovers are cited one by one in the hardware catalog, each with its status label. The full lists, with versions and licenses, are in the repository: backend/docs/SOURCES-horizon.md, planner/SOURCES-planner.md, tools/models/SOURCES-models.md and web/SOURCES-web.md.

Common Horizon is not endorsed by NASA or by any company whose hardware it names.
